standard.title: Forces and Motion
standard.description: investigate and represent balanced and unbalanced forces, including gravitational force, acting on objects, and relate changes in an object's motion to its mass and the magnitude and direction of forces acting on it
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can identify pushes and pulls as forces and know that gravity pulls objects toward Earth. They have not represented forces as vectors, analysed balanced/unbalanced states, or applied F=ma reasoning.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students represent and explain how balanced and unbalanced forces, including gravity, relate to changes in an object's motion in terms of mass, magnitude and direction.

nodes.label: Forces as vectors: magnitude and direction
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can represent forces on an object as vectors showing correct magnitude and direction and name the forces
nodes.minimum_width: Represent at least two forces on an object using arrows with correct relative size and direction; name the forces
nodes.typical_width: Draw force diagrams for 4 different scenarios (stationary, accelerating, decelerating, falling); justify arrow choices
wider: Measure the magnitude of forces using a force meter; represent magnitude and direction using force arrow diagrams
Analyse a real photograph of an object in motion — identify all forces acting and represent them in a diagram
Investigate forces acting on boomerangs and how First Peoples of Australia designed an aerofoil profile — represent forces involved

Limited width — representing forces as vectors is a precision skill that does not vary meaningfully across contexts. More scenarios build fluency but the conceptual content is fixed. The genuine width comes at later nodes where force diagrams are used as reasoning tools.

response_modes.reason: Representing forces as vectors — correct arrow direction, relative size, and force naming — is a precision skill students commonly approximate. They confuse spacing and direction, or omit forces (e.g. normal force). Repeated practice with feedback on diagram completeness and accuracy is what helps, not broader contexts.

success_criteria: Represents at least 2 forces on an object with correct arrow direction and relative size
Diagram is consistent with the described scenario
nodes.hinge_reason: Force diagram errors — wrong arrow direction, omitted forces, incorrect relative sizes — propagate into every subsequent node. Nodes 2-5 all require accurate force diagrams as reasoning tools; students with imprecise diagrams cannot correctly identify balanced/unbalanced states.

nodes.label: Balanced forces and equilibrium
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify whether forces on an object are balanced or unbalanced and predict the resulting motion state
nodes.minimum_width: Define balanced forces; correctly identify whether forces are balanced in a given diagram; state that balanced forces mean no change in motion
nodes.typical_width: Analyse 6 scenarios — classify each as balanced or unbalanced; predict the motion state for each with reasoning
wider: Analyse the effect of balanced and unbalanced forces on an object's motion including starting, stopping and changing direction
Investigate a real engineering structure (e.g. bridge, building) — identify how balanced forces are maintained and what happens if equilibrium is disturbed
Investigate how simple machines such as levers and pulleys change the magnitude of force needed — represent forces involved and identify whether forces are balanced

response_modes.reason: The misconception that balanced forces mean no forces — rather than equal and opposite forces — is extremely common and propagates into every subsequent node. Students who hold this misconception cannot correctly predict motion states or apply Newton's First Law. Working across multiple scenario types (stationary, moving at constant velocity, engineering structures) exposes and resolves the misconception — more contexts, not more repetition of the same scenario.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The engineering structure direction offers advancing students genuinely rich application — analysing how real structures maintain equilibrium connects force balance to design principles and requires students to identify all forces in a complex system, not just a simplified two-force scenario.
success_criteria: Correctly identifies balanced vs unbalanced forces in a given diagram
States that balanced forces mean no change in motion — not that no forces are acting
Predicts the motion state from a force diagram
nodes.hinge_reason: The misconception that balanced forces mean no forces acting propagates directly into Node 3 — students who hold it cannot correctly predict motion states or explain why objects at constant velocity have balanced forces.

nodes.label: Unbalanced forces and changes in motion
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain that unbalanced forces cause a change in motion and represent this with force diagrams
nodes.minimum_width: Explain that unbalanced forces cause a change in motion (speed or direction); give two examples with force diagrams
nodes.typical_width: Analyse motion scenarios — identify the unbalanced force, predict the change in motion, draw the force diagram
wider: Investigate the effects of applying different forces to familiar objects of the same and different mass — identify the pattern between force magnitude and rate of motion change
Design a fair test to investigate how the magnitude of an unbalanced force affects the rate of motion change

Investigate forces through the application of traditional tools such as spearthrowers used by First Peoples of Australia — analyse the forces involved and how tool design optimises the unbalanced force

response_modes.reason: Students frequently apply unbalanced force reasoning only to obvious acceleration scenarios (car speeding up) and miss direction changes (turning, projectile) or deceleration as force-caused changes. Multiple motion-change contexts — starting, stopping, turning, falling — build the generalised understanding that any change in motion requires an unbalanced force.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The fair test design direction gives advancing students genuine investigative richness — designing a test to isolate the effect of force magnitude on acceleration requires planning controls, identifying variables, and interpreting data as evidence for a relationship. The First Peoples spearthrower direction connects force analysis to cultural design knowledge.
success_criteria: States that unbalanced forces cause a change in motion
Gives 2 examples with correct force diagrams
Identifies both speed and direction as possible changes

nodes.label: Gravitational force and mass
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can distinguish mass from weight, explain gravitational force as dependent on mass, and calculate weight from mass
nodes.minimum_width: Distinguish mass from weight; explain gravitational force as dependent on mass; calculate weight given mass and gravitational field strength
nodes.typical_width: Compare gravitational force on the same object on Earth, the Moon, and Mars — explain differences using gravitational field strength; represent using force diagrams
wider: Investigate how Earth's gravitational force pulls objects to the centre of Earth and how its magnitude relates to mass
Examine how gravity affects objects in space including moons, planets, stars, galaxies and black holes — explain patterns in terms of mass and distance
Evaluate a common misconception (e.g. 'objects fall at different rates based on mass') using experimental evidence; construct a refutation using force diagrams and particle reasoning

response_modes.reason: Mass/weight confusion is the most persistent misconception in this standard — students who conflate the two make systematic errors in force calculations and cannot correctly explain gravitational scenarios. Encountering gravitational force across multiple contexts (Earth, Moon, Mars, space) where mass stays constant but weight changes forces the distinction to become functional rather than definitional.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The space direction — gravity affecting moons, planets, stars and black holes — gives advancing students genuinely rich territory for applying the mass-gravity relationship at astronomical scale. The misconception refutation direction is also rich: constructing an evidence-based argument against a common belief requires integrating force diagram reasoning with experimental data.
success_criteria: Correctly distinguishes mass from weight with definitions
Calculates weight correctly given mass and g
Explains gravitational force as dependent on mass — not just Earth's pull
nodes.hinge_reason: Mass/weight confusion propagates directly into AC9S10U05 (Newton's Laws of Motion) — F=ma is meaningless if students conflate mass and weight, and gravitational force scenarios in Newton's Laws require the distinction to be functional. Students who hold this misconception produce systematically wrong force calculations three years later.

nodes.label: Relating force, mass and motion change
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the qualitative relationship between force, mass and acceleration and interpret data from force investigations
nodes.minimum_width: State the relationship between force, mass and acceleration qualitatively; predict whether a heavier or lighter object will accelerate more under the same force
nodes.typical_width: Analyse data from a force investigation — identify the pattern between force, mass and acceleration; represent graphically
wider: Evaluate a real-world application (e.g. vehicle safety, rocket launch) — explain how engineers manipulate force and mass to achieve desired acceleration outcomes
Investigate how simple machines change force magnitude for a task; analyse the trade-offs between force and distance involved
Analyse the forces acting on a boomerang in flight — explain how design variables (aerofoil shape, mass, throwing force) affect the motion outcome

response_modes.reason: This node integrates force vector representation (Node 1), balanced/unbalanced force reasoning (Nodes 2-3), and gravitational force (Node 4) into a qualitative account of how force, mass and motion change relate. Students who can handle each component separately but cannot reason about which of two objects accelerates more under the same force have not integrated the model.

success_criteria: States the qualitative relationship between force, mass and acceleration
Correctly predicts which object accelerates more under the same force
Identifies the pattern in data from a force investigation
